title: Customer Churn Analysis — Verified Findings Report
executive_summary: Across 749 customers, overall churn stands at 37.65%, with an average monthly fee of $42.11. Churn varies little by plan or signup cohort, but contract type is the standout driver: Monthly contracts churn at 48.32% versus 21.85% for Annual, a 121.11% relative increase. An at-risk segment of 100 customers with heavy support contact and low satisfaction churns at 71.0%. Plan tier strongly affects value rather than churn: Premium customers deliver 292.01% more lifetime value than Basic customers.

key_findings.statement: The cleaned dataset contains 749 customers. Overall churn stands at 37.65%, and the average monthly fee is $42.11.
Churn differs little across plans: Basic 38.87%, Standard 36.68%, and Premium 36.60%, with Basic only 2.27 points above Premium. Plan choice alone does not appear to drive churn.
Churn is stable across signup cohorts — 2021: 38.02%, 2022: 36.74%, 2023: 37.05%, 2024: 39.83%. The 2024 cohort is highest, 3.09 points above the lowest cohort (2022).
Contract type is the clearest churn differentiator: Monthly contracts churn at 48.32% versus 21.85% for Annual, a 121.11% relative increase — roughly 2.21x the rate and 26.47 points higher.
The at-risk segment (five or more support tickets and a satisfaction score of 2 or lower) comprises 100 customers, 13.35% of the base, and churns at 71.0% — 33.35 points above the overall churn rate.

Customer tenure averages 20.81 months (median 19.0, standard deviation 13.25), indicating a wide spread of customer lifespans. Average satisfaction is 3.42; 27 customers, or 3.6% of the base, have no satisfaction score.
Average lifetime value climbs steeply by plan: Basic $463.46, Standard $868.83, and Premium $1,816.78. Premium customers are worth 292.01% more than Basic — about 3.92x the value.

limitations: The analysis is descriptive and correlational; no causal claims can be made. For example, Annual-contract customers may simply be lower-risk buyers rather than being retained by the contract itself.
Satisfaction scores are missing for a subset of customers, and the at-risk definition excludes anyone without a score, so the true size of that segment may be understated.
No statistical significance tests or confidence intervals were computed, so the small churn differences between plans and cohorts may reflect random variation rather than real effects.
Findings come from a single customer snapshot; tenure, seasonality, and time-to-churn dynamics are not captured.
conclusion: Retention efforts should prioritize shifting Monthly customers toward Annual contracts, which show far lower churn, and proactively engaging the 100 at-risk customers, who churn at 71.0%. Plan tier has little effect on churn, but Premium accounts carry 292.01% higher lifetime value than Basic, so retaining high-tier customers delivers outsized returns.
